# Fatality model report

*Generated by `src/model_fatality.py` on 2026-10-29. Re-run it after each data update; do not edit by hand.*

**Question:** among U.S. general aviation accidents, which circumstances go with the accident being fatal?
This is about how bad an accident is once it happens, not how likely a flight is to have one.

## Data and method

- 78,861 U.S. general aviation accidents (one row per event, 1982 onward; the same set as `dbo.vw_ga_accident`).
- Trained on 1982-2018 (70,129 accidents), tested on 2019 onward (8,732), so the scores show performance on years the model never saw.
- Inputs: phase of flight, weather (the NTSB's VMC/IMC call), light, aircraft category, engines, amateur-built, type of operation, pilot hours and age, decade, and narrative accident-type tags. Damage, injuries and NTSB findings are left out because they describe the outcome.
- Two models: logistic regression (gives each factor an odds ratio) and gradient boosting (a flexible benchmark).

## How well it predicts (test years)

| Model | ROC AUC | PR AUC | Brier score |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Logistic regression | 0.837 | 0.588 | 0.100 |
| Gradient boosting | 0.843 | 0.596 | 0.100 |
| Baseline (always guess the average) | 0.500 | 0.167 | 0.139 |

ROC AUC is the chance the model ranks a random fatal accident above a random non-fatal one (0.5 = guessing, 1.0 = perfect).
16.7% of test-year accidents were fatal. The simple model is within 0.02 of the flexible one, so its odds ratios are a fair summary.

## Factors that go with fatal outcomes

Odds ratio = how the odds of a fatal outcome compare with the reference level, **holding the other factors equal**. 2.0 means double the odds; 0.5 means half. Odds are not probabilities: when the reference level is rarely fatal, ratios get large, so read them next to the fatal share. Only levels with at least 200 accidents are shown, and "unknown" levels are left out; every level is in `dbo.model_fatality_factor`.

| Factor | Level | Odds ratio | Accidents | Fatal share |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Phase of flight | Maneuvering (vs. Takeoff) | 13.05 | 10,800 | 38.3% |
| Narrative: impairment | Yes (vs. No) | 10.73 | 603 | 80.1% |
| Narrative: stall | Yes (vs. No) | 6.60 | 2,013 | 56.4% |
| Narrative: spatial disorientation | Yes (vs. No) | 6.07 | 772 | 91.3% |
| Phase of flight | Emergency (vs. Takeoff) | 5.34 | 643 | 24.9% |
| Weather (NTSB) | IMC (vs. VMC) | 4.63 | 4,699 | 63.8% |
| Phase of flight | Enroute (vs. Takeoff) | 4.30 | 15,548 | 28.0% |
| Narrative: loss of control | Yes (vs. No) | 3.74 | 2,961 | 48.8% |
| Phase of flight | Initial climb (vs. Takeoff) | 3.36 | 9,721 | 21.2% |
| Phase of flight | Approach (vs. Takeoff) | 2.94 | 9,665 | 23.8% |
| Narrative: cfit | Yes (vs. No) | 2.80 | 460 | 60.9% |
| Aircraft category | Gyroplane (vs. Airplane) | 2.51 | 450 | 33.8% |

## Read with care

- These are associations, not causes. Phase, weather and accident type are linked to each other and to things the data does not record (speed and angle at impact, terrain, survival equipment).
- Narrative tags come from the investigators' text and keyword rules that undercount; older narratives are terser.
- Weather is the NTSB investigator's VMC/IMC call only; observed station weather is on hold (see `enrich_weather.py`).
